questions.question: Explain how the materials list is derived from the parts list and what it contains, describe how the tools list is derived and what it includes, and state how both lists are checked.
questions.expected_answer: The materials list groups the parts list's entries by material and totals what must be collected: metres of dowel with cuts planned from stock lengths to minimise waste, numbers of craft sticks, card of stated thickness for the base box and gear plate, string for rope and guides, gears from the kit by tooth count and quantity, motor, battery holder, switch and wire, the sheave wheel, glues chosen for each joint type, and pins or small screws, each with a small spare for breakages. The tools list follows from the operations each part needs: saw and bench hook or clamp with a mitre box for dowel, craft knives with steel rules and cutting mats for sticks and card, scissors for string, file or sandpaper and a hand drill or awl for shaft holes, pencils, steel rule, set square and try square for marking out, glue gun, PVA, clamps or pegs and pliers for joining, spring balance, stopwatch, ruler and test masses for testing, and eye protection; it doubles as the sign-out sheet. Both are checked against the class store before the build and against the drawing, budget and parts list in the bid so that every part has a material and every joint has a tool.

questions.question: State the question that fixes the order of construction steps, give a logical sequence for building an A-frame headgear model, and identify which steps can run in parallel and which are strict dependencies.
questions.expected_answer: Each step is checked against the question of what must already exist for it to happen. A sequence: cut and label all dowel legs, back-leg and beams; cut diagonals and base members; assemble the base square with its plate and gear plate position; drill the gear plate at the centre distances from the gear drawing, fit shafts dry, check the gears turn freely and test the motor; assemble the two tower faces flat on the bench, glued, clamped and checked square; stand the faces and join them with cross members and remaining diagonals, checking plumb; fit the tower to the base; fit the back-leg from its foot to its top; fit the sheave beam and sheave on its axle; fit drum, gears and motor, string the rope over the sheave to the cage and fit guides; fit the brake, bumper and depth pointer; test lifts with increasing load and adjust; finish, label and photograph. Cutting dowel and cutting card, drilling the gear plate while faces set, and making the cage can run in parallel; standing the faces must follow their assembly, fitting the tower must follow the base and the tower, and the sheave beam must follow the tower, with glue drying placed so other work fills it.

questions.question: Describe the symbols and decision points of the construction flow chart, how the build timetable allocates people and time, and why the list, sequence, flow chart and timetable must agree.
questions.expected_answer: The flow chart uses a rounded box for start and end, rectangles for steps, diamonds for decisions with yes and no arrows, and parallel branches that rejoin; it starts with materials collected, tools signed out and drawing revision checked, branches where the gear plate and tower faces are built together, and places decisions at tests: gears turn freely with a no branch to adjust mesh, tower plumb and square with a no branch to adjust before glue sets, and lifts 300 grams in 10 to 20 seconds with a no branch to check batteries, drum, friction and ratio, ending with the model tested, labelled and photographed. The timetable divides two double periods of about 90 minutes into 15 minute blocks against team members, allocating parallel steps to different people, placing glued assemblies before breaks so they set, staggering use of the hot glue station, and leaving about 30 minutes for adjustment and recording after the first test lift. The four documents are views of one plan: a flow chart step with no materials listed, a tool missing for a joint, or a timetable that places a step before its dependency reveals an error to be corrected before the build.
